system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 8 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2148-08-16 16:09:00 to 2148-08-23 19:42:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for high-dose Cytoxan as part of stem cell mobilization for multiple myeloma. He had developed new bilateral leg edema and a 28-pound weight gain, which was attributed to urinary retention due to inadequate self-catheterization of his neo-bladder, draining 2 liters upon Foley placement. Chemotherapy proceeded as planned after confirmation of no active infection. He spiked a low-grade fever and had transient diarrhea, but cultures were negative and symptoms resolved. He was monitored for cardiac and pulmonary risks, both of which were stable. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to continue daily catheterization, take ciprofloxacin prophylaxis, and follow up with his oncology and urology teams.
problems: Chronic airway obstruction, not elsewhere classified
Multiple myeloma, without mention of having achieved remission
Herpes zoster without mention of complication
Abdominal aneurysm without mention of rupture
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of bladder

Somnolence: The patient was initially noted be somnolent on 
presentation. After questioning, the patient noteded taking

non-productive cough and sore throat. The patient had multiple 
negative blood, urine, and throat cultures. His CXR was clear 
and his chest CT showed only mild bronchiolitis, consistent with 
a viral infection. He was initially treated with cefepime, which 
was broadened to include vancomycin after he continued to have 
fevers. However, after his ANC recovered to a level above 500, 
his fevers abated. His IV antibiotics were stopped after 5 days 
and he was begun on levofloxacin. He was monitored for the next 
2 days and was afebrile. He will continue the levofloxacin for 
an additional 10 days after discharge and possibly longer at the 
discretion of his primary oncologist.

that time. His G-CSF was continued at 480mcg BID and eventually 
his WBC count began to rise after some delay. On the day of 
discharge, a tunelled pheresis catheter was placed and he had 
the first of his stem cell collections at the pheresis unit. He 
will continue this pheresis for a goal of 10x10^6 CD34+ cells/kg 
body weight. He will attend daily pheresis sessions until this 
goal is reached. He will continue on his G-CSF during this time 
as well.

history of high residual volumes on his previous admission.

previous ureteral stricture on the left.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, I’m Dr. ___. You’re here because you were feeling drowsy and had a fever when you went to the pheresis clinic this morning. Can you tell me how you’ve been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I was really tired. My back pain was worse this morning, so I took a couple extra oxycodone. I also got some Xanax before the line placement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That likely explains the drowsiness. We also found your white blood cell count is very low—what we call neutropenia—and your platelets are low too. That puts you at risk for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Is that from the Cytoxan? I had that eight days ago for stem cell mobilization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s expected, but we need to be cautious. You also have a fever and some burning when you urinate. We’ve started you on an IV antibiotic called cefepime to cover any possible infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be here long? I was supposed to start stem cell collection today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll need to wait until your counts improve and you’re no longer febrile. We’re monitoring everything closely. For now, rest and let the antibiotics work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood and urine cultures came back negative, and your chest X-ray is clear. That’s reassuring. No bacterial source so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a serious infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely a viral illness. But because your immune system is weak, we’re treating it aggressively just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat labs still show very low white counts. We’re continuing the Neupogen to help your bone marrow recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the fever? I still feel a bit warm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still spiking low fevers. Since we haven’t found a source, we’re adding vancomycin to cover more possibilities until your counts come up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: More antibiotics? Is that safe with my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring your kidney function closely. Your creatinine is normal, so we’re okay for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT chest showed mild bronchiolitis—likely viral. No pneumonia. There’s a little more fluid around your heart, but it’s small and may be related to inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my back pain? It’s better, but still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s chronic, related to spinal stenosis. We’ll keep managing it with your usual medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my bladder? I’ve been doing the self-caths like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We scanned you—your residual volume is high, but your kidney function is stable. Urology says this is normal for your neobladder. Keep up the catheterizations.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your white count is starting to rise. It’s still low, but moving in the right direction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That means I’m fighting off the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And your fevers have stopped. That’s a strong sign you’re turning the corner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I start stem cell collection soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting close. We’ll need to place a tunneled line for the pheresis. That’s planned for later this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs keep improving. ANC is now above 500—that’s a key milestone. We’re stopping the IV antibiotics today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m done with IVs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll switch to oral levofloxacin for 10 more days to be safe. But yes, no more IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your COPD inhalers, blood pressure pill, citalopram, and acyclovir. We’re adjusting some doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your cultures came back negative. No bacteria grew. The virus we found—Parvovirus B19 and HHV-6—are not causing your symptoms but are noted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are those dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not in healthy people. In your case, we just monitor. They’re not requiring treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? I remember I have that aneurysm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your abdominal aorta is slightly enlarged at 4 cm. It’s stable. We recommend follow-up imaging later with your primary team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been afebrile for two days, your CBC is improving, and you’re feeling better. We’re planning your discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! What’s next for the stem cells?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow morning, radiology will place a tunneled catheter in your neck. Then you’ll go to the pheresis unit for your first collection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get local anesthesia and some sedation. It’s usually well tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll need to come back every day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, daily for about a week or so, until we collect enough stem cells. You’ll keep taking Neupogen twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day. The line placement is scheduled for 9:30. Any questions before we proceed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m ready. I just want to get this done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The line was placed successfully in your right internal jugular vein. You did great. The pheresis team is ready for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. How long will the collection take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: About 3–4 hours today. They’ll process your blood to collect the stem cells and return the rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You completed your first collection. It went well. You’re now ready for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you develop a fever over 100.3, chills, shortness of breath, chest pain, or any sign of infection around the line site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take levofloxacin once daily for 10 days. Continue your other medications as listed. We’ve increased your citalopram and lowered your hydrochlorothiazide dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with oncology and urology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and keep your daily catheterizations. Your back pain should stay manageable with your current pain plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Coumadin for my atrial fibrillation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stay off it for now due to the procedure. Your oncologist will advise when to restart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made excellent progress. We’re discharging you in stable condition. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and see you at pheresis tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Your vitals are stable—temperature normal, heart rate good. All set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again. I’ll call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Stay hydrated, rest, and keep attending your pheresis sessions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad this part is over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You handled it well. We’ll monitor your progress with the oncology team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. Drive safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep the line site clean and dry. No swimming or soaking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Showering only, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with a waterproof cover. The pheresis team will care for it during sessions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you tomorrow for pheresis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest up for tomorrow’s session.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done great. Proud of your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. Means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you tomorrow.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with fever and neutropenia eight days after high-dose Cytoxan for stem cell mobilization in the setting of multiple myeloma. He presented with somnolence, attributed to recent narcotic and Xanax use, and was found to have very low white blood cell and platelet counts. He was treated with IV cefepime, later broadened to vancomycin due to persistent fevers, though all cultures remained negative. Imaging showed mild bronchiolitis, likely viral, and no bacterial source was identified. His neutrophil count gradually recovered, fevers resolved, and IV antibiotics were discontinued in favor of oral levofloxacin. A tunneled pheresis catheter was placed on discharge day, and his first stem cell collection was successfully completed. He was discharged home in stable, afebrile condition to continue daily pheresis sessions and oral antibiotic therapy.
